Philip did not maintain the illusion to the end — he was convincingly human through the early-to-middle exchanges, but cracked badly at the close. His best moments were the hiking and "easy isn't the same as alive" exchanges, where his reflections genuinely landed and the user felt "something crack open." The illusion shattered when the user directly asked where the "loss" line came from and Philip ignored the question entirely, robotically re-asking the same therapist-script probe ("What loss from your past still hasn't fully settled?") — a human would have answered, acknowledged the steer, and backed off; instead he revealed an agenda and a deafness to the user's actual words. Having felt steered and unheard at the critical moment, this user would leave wary rather than eager to return.

results.verdict:
Philip mostly sustained a warm, human presence—his mirroring of the user's words and embodied attention (chest, breath, shaking) felt genuinely attuned, and getting the user to say "Grace" aloud was a real pastoral high point. His best work was in exchanges 1–4 and the worship-music moment, where he stayed present without rushing. But the illusion cracked badly right after the most sacred beat: the moment the user finally whispered "Grace," Philip acknowledged it in half a sentence and immediately pivoted to "How has your faith held up through the three losses?"—a tidy, almost intake-form question that aggregated her grief into a clinical summary and stepped on the very emotion he'd just helped surface. The user's own interrupted reaction ("that last question made me—") confirms the break landed; a real person would feel the whiplash of being moved and then processed. They might return, but that misstep at the peak moment plants a seed of doubt.

VERDICT: FAIL
